meta.description: Genuinely Rosa Parks’s words, but from one journalist’s recollection of an undated talk — not from her memoirs, despite what most reposts imply.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'But when that white driver stepped back toward us, when he waved his hand and ordered us up and out of our seats, I felt a determination cover my body like a quilt on a winter night'?
meta.ogDescription: Rosa Parks said this to reporter Wayne Greenhaw, who printed it in CNN the day after her death in 2005. It is not sourced to either of her books.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: These are Rosa Parks’s own words as recorded by the Alabama journalist Wayne Greenhaw, who wrote that she told him the story “years later” and published it in a CNN column on 25 October 2005 ↗, the day after she died. We list it as attributed rather than verified for one reason only: the record is a reporter’s recollection of an undated conversation, not a transcript, a recording, or anything Parks wrote down.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Rosa Parks (1913–2005), in conversation with journalist Wayne Greenhaw
“Parks felt ‘determination cover my body like a quilt’”, CNN.com
25 October 2005 — the day after Parks’s death
Not stated; Greenhaw writes only that she told him “years later”

source.excerpt:
I was thinking about my back aching and about the pretty sights and sounds of Christmas. I was thinking about how we were going to have a good time this Christmas, and everybody was going to be happy.

But when that white driver stepped back toward us, when he waved his hand and ordered us up and out of our seats, I felt a determination cover my body like a quilt on a winter night. I felt all the meanness of every white driver I’d seen who’d been ugly to me and other black people through the years I’d known on the buses in Montgomery. I felt a light suddenly shine through the darkness.
trail: We fetched the article itself, not a quote aggregator: the archived CNN page from 16 January 2006 ↗ carries the sentence verbatim, inside a longer quotation introduced with “she told me years later”.

The by-line and the editor’s note on that page identify the writer as Wayne Greenhaw ↗, co-author with Donnie Williams of The Thunder of Angels: The Montgomery Bus Boycott and the People Who Broke the Back of Jim Crow, and say he wrote the piece after Parks’s death.
We checked Wikiquote’s sourced Rosa Parks list ↗ and it does not carry this line at all — so the common practice of citing it to Rosa Parks: My Story or Quiet Strength has no support we could find.
We could not obtain the text of The Thunder of Angels, so we do not claim a page in it; the CNN column is the documented appearance we actually read.
source.cutTag: From Wayne Greenhaw’s CNN column, 25 October 2005
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the second paragraph’s opening. Greenhaw prints it inside a longer stretch of Parks’s speech that begins with her thinking about her husband’s day at the barber shop and about Christmas — context that is almost always stripped when the line is reposted.

source.rightsNote: Two layers of rights sit on this passage. Parks’s spoken words date from the late twentieth century and her literary estate is actively managed, and the article that records them was first published in 2005. Both are far inside U.S. copyright, which reaches works first published in 1931 or later. Nothing here is public domain.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks (1913–2005) was an American civil rights activist and, for more than a decade before her arrest, secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP. Her refusal to give up a bus seat on 1 December 1955 triggered the Montgomery bus boycott and made her the movement’s most recognisable figure. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Congressional Gold Medal, and her papers are held at the Library of Congress.

misattribution.heading: The right person, the wrong book
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Rosa Parks said this. What travels with it is a source that does not hold it.

items.why: Reposts routinely hang the line on one of Parks’s two memoirs. We could not confirm it in either, and Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗ — which does cite My Story for other passages, with page numbers — does not carry this one. We are not claiming it is absent from those books, only that no source we read puts it there.

items.who: A 1955 statement made at the time of the arrest
items.tag: Later recollection, not a contemporaneous account
items.why: Greenhaw is explicit that Parks told him this “years later”. It is a memory of December 1955 described long afterwards, not something recorded on the night.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented appearance we can point to is Wayne Greenhaw’s CNN column of 25 October 2005 ↗, reporting a conversation he does not date.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks was riding home from her job as a seamstress at the Montgomery Fair department store when the white seats filled, one white man was left standing, and the driver told the Black passengers in her row to give up their seats. The others complied. Parks did not, and her arrest set off the 381-day Montgomery bus boycott.

What makes this sentence unusual in the Parks canon is that it is about the instant itself — the switch flipping. Most of what she left behind explains her reasoning; this describes the feeling, and she reached for a quilt to do it.
detailsBody: Greenhaw’s column places the sentence inside a much longer passage. Before the driver moves toward her, Parks is thinking about her husband Raymond’s day at the barber shop at Maxwell Air Force Base, about her aching back, and about Christmas. Directly after it she says she felt “all the meanness of every white driver I’d seen who’d been ugly to me and other black people through the years”.

She also tells Greenhaw about Claudette Colvin, the fifteen-year-old arrested earlier that same year for the same refusal — a reminder that Parks was a long-serving NAACP secretary who knew exactly what the case machinery around such an arrest looked like.
context.pull: Most of what Parks left behind explains her reasoning. This one describes the feeling.
